newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan assembly passes anti-terrorism bill.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan assembly passes anti-terrorism bill.

text.p: Pakistan's National Assembly (lower house) passed an Anti-Terrorism Bill on Wednesday to give the government sweeping new security powers, including the right for police to shoot suspects on sight.
The opposition Pakistan People's Party, led by Benazir Bhutto, walked out of the assembly in protest.

The controversial bill, due to be submitted to the Senate (upper house) later on Wednesday, is an attempt to stop a wave of killings that has shaken Pakistan in the run-up to Thursday's golden jubilee celebration of 50 years of independence.

More than 225 people have been killed in a feud involving rival wings of an ethnic party in Karachi so far this year, while a vendetta between militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem factions has cost about 140 lives, mostly in Punjab province.

"There is a spate of terrorist activities and commission of heinous offences in Pakistan," said the bill proposed by Interior Minister Shujaat Hussain. "It is necessary that appropriate administrative and judicial measures are adopted."

The bill, sure to become law thanks to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's large majority in the Senate as well as the National Assembly, would let the federal or provincial governments call in the armed forces to help civilian authorities.
It would authorise policemen, or soldiers deployed in such cases, to fire on anyone committing, or believed to be about to commit, a "terrorist" offence.

The security forces would also be allowed to arrest terrorist suspects without a warrant and to search any premises and seize weapons or anything else used or likely to be used in a terrorist offence, again without a warrant.
The bill proposed the death penalty for any terrorist whose action has resulted in a death, and a sentence of between seven years and life imprisonment otherwise.
It would ban "acts intended or likely to stir up sectarian hatred" and punish their perpetrators with sentences of up to seven years.

The bill would enable the government to set up special courts, with police required to complete investigation of cases within seven working days. The courts would have to decide such cases within a further seven days with a similar period for an appellate tribunal to judge appeals against their verdicts.
The federal or provincial governments could declare any association unlawful "in the interest of public order".
Sharif's government has come under intense pressure to halt the bloodletting in Karachi and Punjab, with many newspaper commentators calling for sectarian groups to be banned.
